blocks.orig: Among the birds of Tanzania you find some of the most beautiful, diverse and unique birds in the world. Although the majority of people come to Tanzania for their dream to see the Big Five or the Great Wildebeest Migration, one look at pictures of all the incredible birds of Tanzania will surely make them expand their dreams.
blocks.html: The birds of Tanzania include some of the most beautiful, varied and unusual species on earth. Most visitors arrive with the dream of seeing the Big Five or the Great Wildebeest Migration, but a single glance at photos of Tanzania’s remarkable birdlife is bound to widen that dream.

blocks.orig: Seeing these majestic feathered creatures, big and small, in their natural habitat is an unforgettable experience. In this article, we tapped into the expert knowledge of our birds of Tanzania guides to come up with a top 10 birds of Tanzania. Grab a cup of tea, make yourself comfortable and enjoy!
blocks.html: Watching these splendid feathered animals, large and small, in their own habitat is something you will not forget. For this article we drew on the expertise of our birds of Tanzania guides to put together a top 10 of Tanzanian birds. Pour yourself a cup of tea, settle in and enjoy!

blocks.orig: It is unknown exactly how many bird species exactly can be found in Tanzania, but the estimate is around one thousand different species. Some birds of Tanzania have not been seen in years. Others are around wherever look – and that’s when our birds of Tanzania guides come in helpful on your Tanzania safari!
blocks.html: Nobody knows precisely how many bird species live in Tanzania, though the estimate is around one thousand. Some Tanzanian birds have not been spotted for years, while others appear wherever you look – and that is exactly where our birds of Tanzania guides prove their worth on your Tanzania safari!

blocks.orig: 10 birds you can see on a Tanzania safari
blocks.html: Ten birds to look out for on a Tanzania safari

blocks.orig: Rufous-tailed weaver – Serengeti National Park
blocks.html: Rufous-tailed weaver – Serengeti National Park

blocks.orig: With its 20 to 22 centimetres, chestnut coloured feathers and dark spots, the rufous-tailed weaver might not be the most colourful fellow. However, what makes it unique is that it’s an endemic bird of Tanzania. This means that this beautiful bird is found nowhere else on planet earth. From July to February, the male birds build their nests during the breeding season, often in the baobabs that the Serengeti National Park is famous for.
blocks.html: At 20 to 22 centimetres, with chestnut plumage and dark spots, the rufous-tailed weaver is hardly the most colourful character. What sets it apart is that it’s endemic to Tanzania, meaning this lovely bird lives nowhere else on the planet. During the breeding season, from July to February, the males build their nests, frequently in the baobabs for which the Serengeti National Park is well known.

blocks.orig: Silvery-cheeked hornbill – Lake Manyara National Park
blocks.html: Silvery-cheeked hornbill – Lake Manyara National Park

blocks.orig: The silvery-cheeked hornbill enjoys a very relaxed life and spends each breeding season with just one partner. For their meals, they typically meet up with other couples in fruit-bearing trees, so don’t be surprised: you might see more than 100 hornbills at the same time! And if you want to impress your fellow adventurers with a fun fact: you can easily distinguish between the male and female hornbill by looking at their beaks. Males have a prominent casque over their entire beak, while females have a much shorter one—a fantastic sight for epic pictures of birds of Tanzania.
blocks.html: The silvery-cheeked hornbill leads a very laid-back life and stays with a single partner for each breeding season. At mealtimes they usually gather with other pairs in fruit-bearing trees, so don’t be surprised to see more than 100 hornbills at once! Want a fun fact to impress your travel companions? Male and female hornbills are easy to tell apart by their beaks: the male carries a prominent casque along the whole beak, whereas the female’s is much shorter—a wonderful subject for epic photos of Tanzanian birds.

blocks.orig: Fisher’s lovebird – Serengeti National Park
blocks.html: Fisher’s lovebird – Serengeti National Park

blocks.orig: Even though they are only 14 centimetres in length, and thus belong to the smallest birds of Tanzania, the small Fisher’s lovebird is easy to spot with their bright green and orange plumage. As their name suggests, these parrots take their romantic life seriously: they are monogamous and spend their whole life with one partner. Furthermore, they have mastered the gender-neutral look: looking at their feathers, you cannot tell whether you see a male or female.
blocks.html: Although it measures just 14 centimetres and so ranks among the smallest birds of Tanzania, the little Fisher’s lovebird is easy to pick out thanks to its bright green and orange plumage. True to their name, these parrots take romance seriously: they are monogamous and stay with one partner for life. They have also perfected the gender-neutral look, as their feathers give no clue as to whether you are looking at a male or a female.

blocks.orig: From one of the smallest parrots in Tanzania, to a large bird of prey on top 10 birds of Tanzania. The Tawney eagle has a wingspan of up to 190 centimetres. This eagle is called ‘roofarend’ in Afrikaans, which means ‘robber eagle’. With a diet of carrion, this Tanzania bird is considered quite aggressive when it robs its prey from other birds—a way of feeding that is called kleptoparasitism. So be aware!
blocks.html: From one of Tanzania’s smallest parrots we move to a big bird of prey in our top 10 birds of Tanzania. The Tawney eagle has a wingspan of as much as 190 centimetres. In Afrikaans it is known as the ‘roofarend’, meaning ‘robber eagle’. Feeding on carrion, this Tanzanian bird is regarded as fairly aggressive when it steals prey from other birds—a feeding habit known as kleptoparasitism. So watch out!

blocks.orig: Black heron – Lake Manyara National Park
blocks.html: Black heron – Lake Manyara National Park

blocks.orig: The black heron is an extremely sharp-witted, pitch-black bird with a size of 42 to 66 centimetres. To catch fish it steps into shallow water, bows its head and then spreads its wings around it, forming a feathery canopy. By doing so, he can clearly see what’s going on underwater and catch fish more easily. Sometimes you can also catch the heron hanging around the African sacred ibis. The ibis stirs up the fish through the water, after which the black heron simply swoops in and catches the fish. Fast food on a busy day!
blocks.html: The black heron, a pitch-black bird of 42 to 66 centimetres, is remarkably clever. When fishing it wades into shallow water, lowers its head and wraps its wings around itself, creating a canopy of feathers. This gives it a clear view of what is happening under the surface, making the fish easier to catch. Now and then you may also find the heron keeping company with the African sacred ibis: the ibis stirs the fish up through the water and the black heron simply dives in to grab them. Fast food on a busy day!

blocks.orig: Red and yellow barbet – Tarangire National Park
blocks.html: Red and yellow barbet – Tarangire National Park

blocks.orig: The red and yellow barbet is one of the sweetest birds in Tanzania. Well known for their beautiful (and loud) voices, their singing has a great rhythm to it. Their beautiful songs often last for a full two minutes and are accompanied by calls from other birds. This grand stage also needs a stunning outfit, and with a red head, yellow chest and black wings with white spots, the red, and yellow barbet ticks that box exceptionally well. With so many qualities, it doesn’t even matter that the wingspan of a red and yellow barbet is only around 10 centimetres!
blocks.html: Among the most endearing birds in Tanzania is the red and yellow barbet. It is famous for its beautiful (and loud) voice, and its song has a wonderful rhythm. These songs often go on for a full two minutes, with other birds chiming in. Such a grand performance calls for a striking outfit, and with its red head, yellow chest and black wings dotted with white, the red and yellow barbet more than delivers. With all those qualities, who cares that its wingspan is only around 10 centimetres!

blocks.orig: We all know that female birds sometimes pick their mate based on very specific criteria, like the most original dance or the most beautiful nest. The flamingo, prevalent in Arusha National Park, is one of them. During the mating season, the males get together in a large group. In perfect synchronicity, they flap their wings, turn their heads and sing. After this performance, the couples find each other and subsequently stay together for life. If you’re lucky enough to catch them in this beautiful mating ritual, you will undoubtedly make one of your most beautiful and unique pictures of birds of Tanzania.
blocks.html: As we all know, female birds sometimes choose a mate on very particular grounds, such as the most inventive dance or the finest nest. The flamingo, common in Arusha National Park, is one such bird. In the mating season the males assemble in a big group and, perfectly in time with one another, flap their wings, turn their heads and sing. Once this show is over, the pairs find one another and then remain together for life. Should you be lucky enough to witness this lovely courtship ritual, you are sure to come away with one of your most beautiful and unusual photos of Tanzanian birds.

blocks.orig: Golden-breasted Starling – Mkomazi National Park
blocks.html: Golden-breasted starling – Mkomazi National Park

blocks.orig: During your safari in Mkomazi National Park, make sure to keep your eyes open for the golden-breasted starling. Thanks to its fantastic plumage, it’s a bird that’s not hard to miss. The upper part of this bird is coloured in iridescent blue, green, and purple. The belly is golden-yellow, and to top it off, this starling has a very long tail. Ask your birds of Tanzania guide for the tips to recognise the birds of Tanzania during your luxury safari.
blocks.html: On safari in Mkomazi National Park, keep a lookout for the golden-breasted starling. With plumage this spectacular, it’s a bird that’s hard to overlook. Its upper body shimmers in iridescent blue, green and purple. The belly is golden-yellow and, as a finishing touch, this starling sports a very long tail. Your birds of Tanzania guide can give you tips for recognising Tanzanian birds during your luxury safari.

blocks.orig: You can only find Pel’s fishing owl in countries in Africa. However, you need to be lucky to actually see one. Because, like all nocturnal animals, Pel’s fishing owl only hunts at dusk, dawn, and night. Also, with its red-brownish plumage, it perfectly blends into the trees where it spends most of its day cuddled up with its mate. However, if the owl doesn’t find enough food during the night, you might also see it during the day. So keep your eyes open!
blocks.html: Pel’s fishing owl is found only in African countries, and actually seeing one takes some luck. Like all nocturnal animals, it hunts solely at dusk, dawn and during the night, and its reddish-brown plumage blends in perfectly with the trees where it passes most of the day snuggled up to its mate. If the night’s hunting has not yielded enough food, however, the owl may show itself by day too. So keep your eyes peeled!

blocks.orig: In a top 10 list of Tanzania birds, we cannot miss out on the worlds’ biggest bird: the ostrich! There is much to say about this magnificent bird, but our favourite ostrich facts are:
blocks.html: No top 10 of Tanzanian birds would be complete without the worlds’ largest bird: the ostrich! A great deal could be said about this magnificent creature, but these are our favourite ostrich facts:

blocks.orig: The males have black and white plumage, and the females are brown-greyish.
blocks.html: Males are black and white, while females have brownish-grey plumage.

blocks.orig: With its long legs and a forward kick, it can actually kill a predator like a lion or even a human… theoretically 😉
blocks.html: Thanks to its long legs and a forward kick, it is capable of killing a predator such as a lion, or even a person… in theory 😉

blocks.orig: Contrary to popular belief, ostriches do not bury their heads in the sand.
blocks.html: Despite what many people think, ostriches do not stick their heads in the sand.
